14.0.s.en: 1. The life of man on earth

14.0.0.en: 1 "Man that is born of a woman is of few days, and full of trouble. 2 He cometh forth like a flower, and is cut down: he fleeth also as a shadow, and continueth not. 3 And dost thou open thine eyes upon such an one, and bringest me into judgment with thee? 4 Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? not one. 5 Seeing his days are determined, the number of his months are with thee, thou hast appointed his bounds that he cannot pass; man that is born of a woman is of few days, and full of trouble (wrath) [1].

14.0.1.en: Job agrees with Eliphaz that man is born for toil and hardship. The wise man says, "For all his days are sorrows, and his travail grief; yea, his heart taketh not rest in the night. This is also vanity" (Eccl 2:23). So when a person concentrates on what has befallen him, he looks at life with a bitter eye. But when he lifts his heart to God, he sees in life a divine gift, and he perceives God's plan behind the troubles that befall him, so that his soul rejoices in the spirit of hope.

14.0.2.en: Job looks at himself as at every man, and finds nothing to boast of, for he is born of a woman, that is, of weak human seed. Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that the woman here signifies spiritual weakness, for the man who is born of a woman in weakness is filled with wrath. He is of few days; however long his life, the whole of it is reckoned as few days, and the sum of his whole life is that it is days filled with toil and pain, and rarely does a day pass without distress.

14.0.3.en: * Truly, the state of man is wretched! He is bound to give an account of his sin, and yet he has not been able to avoid sin.

14.0.4.en: He has been compelled to enter into judgment, to stand before the sight of Almighty God, declaring the reasons for his conduct... although no one can be clean from sin.

14.0.5.en: The guilt goes back to the very beginning of childhood, before man has the ability to perceive wrongdoing.

14.0.6.en: What a wretched state this is, that his life is short, temptation is sweet, trials are multiplied, and anger is a daily work. For even in the midst of a moment of joy there is a constant bitterness.

14.0.7.en: St. Ambrose St. Augustine comments on the phrase [full of wrath] (Job 1:14) by saying that the wrath of God is prompted only by His mercies and His love, which moved Him to the incarnation of the only-begotten Son in the fullness of time, in order to renew us and remove from us all the guilt of sins, whether the ancestral sin inherited through the generations or those we ourselves commit.

14.0.8.en: * The human race fell under a just judgment, and all men became children of wrath. Of this wrath it is written: [For all our days are passed away in thy wrath: we spend our years as a tale that is told] (Ps 90:9). And Job also says of this wrath: [Man that is born of a woman is of few days, and full of wrath] (Job 14:1). And of this wrath the Lord Jesus also says: "He that believeth on the Son hath everlasting life: and he that believeth not the Son shall not see life; but the wrath of God abideth on him" [(Jn 3:36) - the words of St. John the Baptist, not of the Lord Christ]... Every man is born with this wrath, therefore the Apostle says, "and were by nature the children of wrath, even as others" (Eph 2:3).

14.0.9.en: St. Augustine * Man is "born of a woman, of few days," because God commanded him to return to the dust (Gen 3:19). As for his being full of wrath, (Job is thinking) of the moment when man received the commandment to keep the commandment and disobeyed it (Gen 2:17; 3:6).

14.0.10.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * Notice the precision of the expression: "treasurest up unto thyself wrath" (Rom 2:5), showing that judgment does not proceed from the Judge, but is the result of the sinner's own work, for he does not say "God treasures up for you," but "you treasure up for yourself"... He tries to draw you by every means, and if you remain in your stubbornness you treasure up for yourself wrath in the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment of God. But do not let it come to your mind that His wrath is a violent passion; it is justice, it is a "revelation," where each man receives what he deserves.

14.0.11.en: St. John Chrysostom * When we read of the wrath and anger of the Lord, we must not understand the word according to the meaning of an ignoble human passion, but in a sense that befits God, who is free from every passion and blemish. Hence we must understand from this that He is the Judge and Avenger of all the unjust things that are committed in this world.

14.0.12.en: And by the logic of these terms and their meaning we ought to fear Him as the One who is to be feared as the Repayer for our deeds, and we ought to fear doing anything against His will. For human nature is accustomed to fear those whom it knows to be angry, and is terrified of offending them, as is the case with some judges who have reached the height of justice.

14.0.13.en: The avenging wrath is usually feared by those who are tormented by the accusation of their consciences, not, of course, because this inclination exists in the minds of those who will keep to equity in their judgments. But while they are in the throes of this fear, the judge's disposition toward them is marked by justice, impartiality and respect for the law he carries out. And this, however gently and kindly he acts, is branded with the harshest terms of anger and fierce wrath by those who have been punished rightly and justly.

14.0.14.en: St. John Cassian St. Gregory of Nyssa sees that Job here calls man "the mortal."

14.0.15.en: * [The mortal, born of a woman, is of few days, and full of wrath] [1]. The being whom the Holy Bible calls "man" in the history of creation... Job calls the very same being mortal, while some of the pagan writers call him a human being, and others "a speaking, articulate creature."

14.1.0.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa He cometh forth like a flower, and withereth: he fleeth also as a shadow, and continueth not [2].

14.1.1.en: Job likens the life of man to two symbols: 1. The flower of the field, or the grass, which appears for a little while and soon dries up because of the heat of the sun and falls (Isa 40:7; Jas 1:11; 1 Pet 1:24). 2. The shadow, as though it had no being, which soon vanishes. As Bildad said, "For our days upon earth are a shadow" (Job 8:9).

14.1.2.en: * He is [like a flower that blooms, then falls after it has been shaken]. Man blossomed in Paradise until he gave names to all the animals (Gen 2:20). But he fell after he was shaken, being drawn away by the deceit of the serpent (Gen 3:4-5; 2 Cor 11:3). After this [he fled like a shadow], for when he found himself naked he fled from God, and hid himself under a tree in Paradise when God called him: [Adam, where art thou?] (Gen 3:7-9). Our hope collapsed, and when man was driven out of Paradise he became corrupt, lost all his help, and perished utterly, so that with one blow he was condemned and driven out, with no hope for us of judgment in our favor.

14.1.3.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * Life in the flesh is a flower in the grass. It was well said by the Psalmist: "As for man, his days are as grass: as a flower of the field, so he flourisheth" (Ps 103:15). Isaiah also says: [All flesh is grass, and all the goodliness thereof is as the flower of the field] (Isa 40:6). For man is like a flower that disappears; suddenly he shows himself on an open day, and in a moment he is drawn away by death, where he disappears...

14.1.4.en: Since man is drawn away daily to death, moment by moment, it was rightly added: [He fleeth as a shadow, and shall not remain in one state]... Why is the life of man likened to a shadow and not to the sun, except because, according to the voice of the Truth: "Because iniquity shall abound, the love of many shall wax cold" (Mt 24:12)?

14.1.5.en: It was well said: [He shall not continue in one state]. For he passes from early infancy to childhood, from childhood to youth, from youth to manhood, from manhood to old age, and from old age to death. So in the present life man is bound, by the very steps of his growth, to diminish. And he is always being destroyed by the very causes by which he thinks he acquires what belongs to his life. For we cannot have a lasting abode here; we came in order to pass through, and by the very means by which we live we pass daily out of this life.

14.1.6.en: The first man was not able to perceive this departure from life, before the disobedience, since time passed over him while he stood firm. But after the disobedience man set himself upon a kind of slope of his temporary state. For when he ate the forbidden fruit he immediately failed to remain.

14.1.8.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that this subjection to external change is accompanied by an inner change as well, as man strives to practice better works. For the mind is always in a state of change, unless a person holds to self-control so as not to descend to a bad state.

14.1.9.en: [The mind that has abandoned the One who stands forever has lost its permanence and its continuing in one state. While it strives to practice better things it is bound to face what opposes the current, but if it slackens in its attempt to ascend, without effort it is carried backward to a state lower than the one it was in.

14.1.10.en: For ascent requires effort, and in descent there is rest from effort. Therefore the Lord warns us to enter by the strait gate, saying: "Strive to enter in at the strait gate" (Lk 13:24)...

14.1.11.en: If there is no striving from a burning heart, the waters of the world are not overcome, and the soul sinks to the lower places.]

14.2.0.en: And dost thou open thine eyes upon such an one, and bringest me into judgment with thee [3]?

14.2.1.en: Job stands amazed that God, who knows that the life of man is like a shadow that does not last but soon vanishes, nevertheless takes such great care to bring Job to judgment.

14.2.2.en: David the Psalmist cried out: [LORD, what is man, that thou takest knowledge of him! or the son of man, that thou makest account of him! Man is like to vanity: his days are as a shadow that passeth away] (Ps 144:3-4). Again he says: "What is man, that thou art mindful of him? and the son of man, that thou visitest him?" (Ps 8:4).

14.2.3.en: In great humility Job sees that he is not worthy for God to scrutinize his faults or to judge him. "And enter not into judgment with thy servant" (Ps 143:2).

14.2.4.en: * Who can be justified in the eyes of God, if the child of one day cannot be cleansed from sin, and no one can boast of his righteousness and the purity of his heart?

14.2.5.en: St. Ambrose * [Hast thou not given him regard, and brought him to judgment before thee?] [3]. This does not concern Adam alone before his disobedience. For God cared for him so that he would not sin and be driven out of Paradise. Therefore He commanded him before he sinned: "Of every tree of the garden thou mayest freely eat: but of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, thou shalt not eat of it: for in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die" (Gen 2:16-17).

14.2.6.en: As for us too, He has given us regard: He gave us the written Law, and added also the Prophets (Mt 11:13).

14.2.7.en: What more could He have said than this? Besides this He gave us the grace of the Gospel (Acts 20:24), through which He showed us how we can receive the original dignity, how we may avoid the threat of Gehenna (Lk 12:5), and also seek Paradise (Mk 13:33).

14.2.8.en: He asked man to enter into judgment, that he might receive the recompense according to his works (Mt 16:27).

14.2.9.en: Since we know all this, we must pass through our life in a sound way, for each one is punished and crowned according to his works. Those who imitate Adam fall under the penalty, since they did not profit from the lesson given for their discipline. But as for those who keep the commandments of the Law, He shows us how they become better by keeping the commandments (Mt 5:19). We shall be worthy to receive a double reward from the just Judge (Mt 5:12), since we are upheld by the grace given to us through the new Adam (Rom 15:15). For this is the way by which we may enjoy happiness in the Kingdom and in the glory of God the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.

14.3.0.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? not one [4].

14.3.1.en: In true humility Job looks at his life as grass that dries up or a shadow that dissolves, and at the same time he sees his life as unclean. Who can bring purity out of this uncleanness?

14.3.2.en: As David the Psalmist cried out: [Behold, I was shapen in iniquity; and in sin did my mother conceive me] (Ps 51:5). No one can purify or sanctify man except his Creator, for the work of purification is like a re-creation. "Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me" (Ps 51:10).

14.3.3.en: Job sees that man bears the corruption of sin from his conception, as the Psalmist says: [In iniquities I was conceived, and in sin did my mother bear me]. It is as though Job were telling God that he is a sinner, because all humanity has been defiled since the fall of our first parents, so everyone needs Your sanctifying and cleansing of them; there is none who is justified before You.

14.3.4.en: * Although the servants and friends of God avoid the sins that lead to death, and practice many good works, we do not believe that they are without trivial sins, for God does not lie when He says: [No child whose life is one day upon the earth is without sin](b). Add to this the blessed John the Evangelist, who is doubtless no less than James in merit, and who declares: [If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us] (1 Jn 8:1). Moreover, we read in another place: "A just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again" (Prov 16:24).

14.3.5.en: Fr. Caesarius, Bishop of Arles * [Who can make clean what has an unclean seed?] He alone who is pure in Himself can cleanse unclean things.

14.3.6.en: For the man who lives in a corrupt body has the uncleanness of temptation rooted in him, since he derives it from his birth. For his very conception is accomplished through an impure fleshly pleasure. The Psalmist says: [In iniquities I was conceived, and in sins did my mother bear me] (Ps 51:5)... Therefore man is tempted against his will. But whoever masters the passions of secret temptations and overcomes the defilement of thought must not ascribe this purity to himself, for no one can make what was conceived in uncleanness become pure except Him who alone is pure in Himself.

14.3.7.en: The meaning here is that the blessed Job was looking toward the incarnation of the Savior, and saw that He alone in the world was not conceived of unclean seed, and so He derived nothing from an unclean conception. For He did not come from the seed of a man and a woman, but from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary. He alone is truly pure in His body, for He did not come into the world according to the pleasure of the flesh.

14.3.9.en: *You quoted the following passage from the Book of Job: "In thy sight no one is clean, even if his life on the earth were one day" (Job 4:14-5) LXX. And you added: "for we are guilty after the likeness of Adam's disobedience," an opinion that your book declares in an honorable and clear way concerning the prophecy of Jonah, where it affirms that the little children of Nineveh were rightly bound to fast with the people merely because of their ancestral sins. Therefore it is not unfitting for me to put the question to you: where did the soul commit the iniquity from which, even at this age, it is bound to be freed by the sacrament of Christian grace?

14.3.10.en: * No man is without sin, whether his life is one day or he lives many years. For if the very stars are not pure in the eyes of God, how much more the worm and the corruption into which those who submitted to the sin of Adam's disobedience have fallen?

14.3.11.en: St. Augustine * [Who shall be cleansed from uncleanness? No one, even if his life on earth is one day] (Job 14:4). No one can boast and say, "I am clean," except Christ "who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth" (1 Pet 2:22).

14.3.12.en: ,The child of one day, in whom there is no uncleanness, because he does not know how to discern the good from the evil (Isa 7:15-16), nevertheless bears the corruption of the old Adam (1 Cor 15:42) that lies upon us. But the grace of the new Adam, who put off the old Adam from us (Eph 4:22; Col 3:9), has also cleansed our corruption [by the washing of regeneration] (Titus 3:5).

14.4.0.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem Seeing his days are determined, the number of his months are with thee, thou hast appointed his bounds that he cannot pass [5].

14.4.1.en: Job looks at his life and finds that even his span of years is determined by God beforehand. God, who has authority and power, determines the age of man by the day and the month, so that he cannot go beyond what is determined for him. Moses the prophet says: "So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom" (Ps 90:12).

14.4.2.en: It is God who [killeth and maketh alive] (2 Kgs 5:7); nothing happens by chance, for the life of man is known to God, and his days are determined with Him.

14.4.3.en: * "Thou hast appointed his bounds (his time) that he cannot pass" (Job 14:5). For all men it has been determined by our Creator, not only by years and months, but also by days and hours. He has "appointed a time," and the time is fixed and can never be passed. Do you not know that many are saved from a deadly sickness, while others in good health are suddenly snatched from this passing life? Some fall from high places and come down safe and sound, while others, as they walk, are snatched away by death at a vain step. Again, some leave their ship (while it is sinking) and climb upon a bare plank, and arrive in health and safety, while others find death near the harbor, their ship sinking there where no one expects death to be their lot, yet it is fulfilled at the call of the Creator.

14.4.4.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * I know that the human soul is spiritual and not bodily, endowed with reason and thought, and that it is not of the substance of God, but created from the life of God, which alone is blessed life; and it is immortal because its sensation must continue forever and form the source of its happiness or woe. Truly, it is not indebted for its being enclosed in the body to works it performed before the body, yet in man it is never without sin, even if its life is one day. Of all those who are born of the offspring of Adam, no man is born without sin. And it is necessary even for infants to be born anew in Christ by the grace of regeneration. I know all this concerning the soul.

14.4.5.en: * Among those born of the offspring of Adam there is no man who was born without sin, and it is necessary even for little infants to be born anew in Christ by the grace of regeneration.

14.4.6.en: St. Jerome * As for the swarm of sins of the soul and of free will, what sermon could proclaim them? He says: "From within... proceed evil thoughts" (Mk 7:21; Mt 15:19). And he adds a list of the thoughts that defile us.

14.4.7.en: If the snares of sins are spread around us on every side, through all the senses and the inner movements of the soul, who can boast that his heart is clean, as Wisdom says (Prov 20:9) LXX? Or as Job testifies to the same thing: "Who is clean from stain?" (Job 14:4) LXX?

14.4.8.en: The stain that attaches to the purity of the soul is sensual pleasure, which is mingled with human life in various ways through the soul and the body, through thoughts, senses, deliberate movements and bodily actions.

14.4.9.en: Then whose soul is clean of this stain?

14.4.10.en: How is there anyone not struck by vainglory and not trodden under the foot of pride?

14.4.11.en: Who has never been shaken by sinful hands, and whose foot has never run to evil?

14.4.12.en: Who has never been corrupted by the wandering of his eyes toward corruption, or of his ears that are not restrained?

14.4.13.en: Who has never been occupied in tasting with pleasure, and whose heart has never been moved by vain passions?

14.4.14.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa * [No one is without stain, even if his life is one day] (Job 14:4). David groans, saying: [In iniquities I was conceived, and in sins did my mother bear me] (Ps 51:5). The Apostle also declares: "For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God; being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus: whom God hath set forth to be a propitiation through faith in his blood" (Rom 3:23-25). Therefore forgiveness of sins is granted to those who believe, since the Lord Himself said: "For this is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins" (Mt 26:28).

14.4.15.en: St. Basil the Great Origen uses this phrase to affirm the necessity of baptizing infants, since no one is without defilement, even if his life is one day (*).

14.4.16.en: * Little children are baptized for the remission of sins (Acts 2:38). Whose sins? When did they commit sins? Or how can the washing of baptism be explained in the case of little children, except according to the interpretation we spoke of a little while ago? [No one is clean from defilement, even if his life upon the earth is one day] (Job 14:4-5). The defilement of birth is removed through the mystery of baptism. This is why even little children are baptized. For except a man be born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter into the Kingdom of Heaven.

14.4.17.en: * Every man who enters this world is said to bear a certain corruption. The Holy Scripture also says this: [No one is clean from defilement (filth), even if his life is only one day] (Job 14:4-5). And this in truth takes place in the womb (Job 3:11) of his mother, when he has received a body from the origin of the parental seed, so that it is said of him that [he was corrupted in his father and mother] (see Lev 21:11). Do you not know that when a male child reaches forty days he is presented at the altar to be purified (Lev 12:2-4), as if he had been defiled in his conception by the parental seed or the womb of his mother? Therefore every man [is defiled in his father and mother] (Lev 21:12).

14.4.18.en: But Jesus alone, my Lord, came into the world pure in this birth of His and was not defiled in His mother, because He entered into an undefiled body. For He is the One who said long ago through Solomon: [Being good, I came into a body undefiled] (Wis 8:20).

14.4.19.en: Origen * No one is clean from sin, even if he lived one day. For the Apostles and the saints did not dare to say: We are holy. Nor did they dare to say, "I have pleased" but "I will please." The prophet promises concerning the future and confesses that he has not done so in the past: "I will please the Lord." Where did he please the Lord? "In the land of the living" (Ps 116:9). This land is the land of the dead; the other land is the land of the living.

14.4.20.en: * Hold the feet of the Savior. Wash them with your tears, and wipe them with your hair. When you do this you reach His head. When you go down into the spring of life with the Savior, then you learn to pour the ointment on the head of the Savior. If Christ is the head of every man (1 Cor 11:3), your head must be anointed, and after your baptism you are anointed.

14.4.21.en: St. Jerome * [In iniquities I was conceived] (Ps 51:5). Was David born of fornication, being born of Jesse (1 Sam 18:16), a righteous man, and his wife? What does he say about himself but those iniquities that came from Adam? Even the bond of death has been planted in the soul with iniquity itself?

14.4.22.en: For no man is born without punishment being brought with him; the deserving of punishment is brought with him.

14.4.23.en: A prophet says in another place: [No one is clean in thy sight, even if he were a child whose life is one day upon the earth] (Job 5:14) LXX.

14.4.24.en: St. Augustine *Those who want to offer an excuse for their sins claim that there is no one without sin. They resort to the testimony of the Book of Job where he says: "No one is clean from filth, even if his life upon the earth is one day. The number of his months can be counted" (Job 14:4-5) LXX.

14.4.25.en: They merely utter this phrase and are wholly ignorant of its meaning. We answer them briefly. For a man to be without sin has two meanings in the Holy Bible. One is that a man has never sinned, and the other is that he ceases to commit sin.

14.4.26.en: If they say that this phrase "without sin" means that there is no one who has never sinned, we agree with them, for there is no one without sin. We all sinned at some time, even if we became virtuous afterward.

14.4.27.en: But if they take the text to mean that they deny that a person after he sins can practice the virtues and no longer return to sin, then this opinion of theirs is wrong. For it can happen that a man who formerly sinned stops sinning and is said to be "without sin."

14.4.28.en: Our Lord Jesus Christ [presented to himself a glorious church, not having spot] (Eph 5:27), not because the members of the Church never had any stain, but because they were lately freed from stain. The Scripture adds: "or wrinkle," not because the members of the Church never at any time had the wrinkle of the old man (Eph 4:22; Col 3:9), but because they have ceased to be so.

14.4.29.en: Origen * This also can be taken concerning the spirit, for we sometimes try to advance in attaining gains in virtue and some of the gifts offered to us, but we are prevented from some of them... For there is no man who reaches the degree he desires, but Almighty God, who discerns what is within us, sets limits to the spiritual gains themselves. So in the matters over which a man tries to rule and is unable, he no longer boasts even of the things that are within his power.

14.4.30.en: This is the reason why the great preacher who was caught up to the third heaven and pierced the walls of Paradise (2 Cor 12), after receiving this revelation, was not given authority to rest and to be without temptation, but because Almighty God [appointed to man his bounds that he cannot pass], He raised him to perceive heavenly things, then brought him down again to submit to weaknesses. This happened so that he would not be proud of himself, but would keep to humility, and so keep within his limits, and after looking at the measure of his limits would seek to be in safety.

14.4.32.en: The Septuagint reads: "No man is clean from stain (filth)." Origen comments on this by saying that the text does not say: "No man is clean from sin," but "from filth." [For every soul that has put on the human body has its filth, but Jesus accepted this willingly, taking the human body for our salvation (bearing in it our stains). [Listen to Zechariah the prophet; he says: [Now Joshua was clothed with filthy garments] (Zech 3:3). Zechariah says this in order to answer those who deny that our Lord took a true body, and claim that His body was of heavenly, spiritual matter.

14.4.33.en: Origen comments on this phrase by saying that none of the saints holds a celebration of his birthday. On the contrary, we find in the Old Testament that Pharaoh held a celebration of his birth, and at the feast he killed the chief baker and hanged him (Gen 40:20-22), and Herod made a feast on his birthday and beheaded St. John the Baptist.

14.5.0.en: 6 Turn from him, that he may rest, till he shall accomplish, as an hireling, his day. 7 "For there is hope of a tree, if it be cut down, that it will sprout again, and that the tender branch thereof will not cease. 8 Though the root thereof wax old in the earth, and the stock thereof die in the ground; 9 Yet through the scent of water it will bud, and bring forth boughs like a plant. 10 But man dieth, and wasteth away: yea, man giveth up the ghost, and where is he? 11 As the waters fail from the sea, and the flood decayeth and drieth up: 12 So man lieth down, and riseth not: till the heavens be no more, they shall not awake, nor be raised out of their sleep. 13 "O that thou wouldest hide me in the grave, that thou wouldest keep me secret, until thy wrath be past, that thou wouldest appoint me a set time, and remember me! 14 If a man die, shall he live again? all the days of my appointed time will I wait, till my change come. 15 Thou shalt call, and I will answer thee: thou wilt have a desire to the work of thine hands.

14.5.1.en: Turn from him, that he may rest, till he shall accomplish, as an hireling, his day [6].

14.5.2.en: Since the affliction has grown severe upon him, which Job considers to be by God's permission, he asks Him to lift His hand from him so that he may rest from the severity of what has befallen him. As the Psalmist says: "O spare me, that I may recover strength, before I go hence, and be no more" (Ps 39:13).

14.5.3.en: It is as though he says to God: even my best days are full of toil and misery, so allow me to breathe from the continual distress. The hireling looks with hope to the end of his day, to rest from his labor. Count my days as the days of a hireling! Let there be toil in them, but let there be intervals of rest between them.

14.5.4.en: * "Turn from him (for a while), that he may rest, till he shall accomplish, as an hireling, his day" [6]. By "turn from him" he means here: remove from him the violence of the blow. But who can rest if he is far from (God), since God alone is rest? And as far as man departs from Him, he departs from rest?

14.5.5.en: As far as the hireling is from the end of his work, so far is he from the reward of his wages. Therefore every saint who is in this life, while he sees that he is far from departing from the present life, grieves that he is far from the eternal blessing.

14.5.7.en: For there is hope of a tree.

14.6.0.en: If it be cut down, that it will sprout again, and that the tender branch (its boughs) thereof will not cease [7].

14.6.1.en: Job looks at his life on earth, which is a single life that, once it passes, does not return, while the tree, if it is cut down and its root is left in the soil, puts forth small branches, as though it were newly planted. For the moisture of the earth and the rains of heaven act upon its trunk so that it breathes and lives anew, but man, once he is buried in the grave, does not rise in this world.

14.6.2.en: Job sees that life is better for trees than for man, for when a tree falls, a new tree can sprout from its trunk. When the prophet Isaiah prophesied about the restoration of the cities of Judah after their ruin, he offered the following comparison: "But as the terebinth and the oak, which even when cut down have a stock, whose stock shall be a holy seed" (Isa 6:13). For the house of Jesse - that is, Israel - is cut down, as a great oak (holm oak) is cut down. But God in His great mercy allows the stump of this oak to sprout again and bring forth a glorious new branch, the Messiah the Savior, who is from the tribe of Judah. "And there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots: and the spirit of the LORD shall rest upon him..." (Isa 11:1-2).

14.6.3.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) offers us a prophetic interpretation, seeing in these words a prophecy of the death and resurrection of the Lord Christ.

14.6.4.en: * He was able to die by His sufferings, but by the glory of His resurrection He came again to the greenness of life. His branches that sprout are the believers in Him, who are multiplied by His resurrection and so grow and spread. His root appears as one that has grown old in the earth, since the preaching of Him to the unbelieving Jews was a disgraceful matter. [His stock died in the dust](c), where now are the hearts of His persecutors, held by the spirit of their unbelief, so that He became as one despised and rejected, because He was able to die in the body. But [through the scent of water it budded](d) by the power of God, and His body after His death rose from the dead. This is as it is written: "whom God hath raised from the dead" (Acts 3:15)... [and put forth leaves like a new plant], since the weakness of the Apostles, who feared at the time of His death, and became dry through their denial of Him, was revived anew in faith by the glory of His resurrection. In comparison with this tree, what is every man but dust?

14.6.6.en: * If there is hope for the visible tree of new life even after it is cut down, as long as its root is firm, how much more for the tree endowed with reason? Just as there is an axe for this tree, there is also an axe for the tree that has reason (Lk 3:9).

14.7.0.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem Though the root thereof wax old in the earth, and the stock thereof die in the ground [8].

14.7.1.en: * What is the root of the righteous man but the holy preaching, since it is his source, to which he holds fast? And what does he mean by the earth or the dust but the sinner? To whom it was said by the voice of the Creator: [Dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return](e). So the root of the righteous man [waxes old in the earth, and his stock dies in the ground]... For according to the words of Wisdom: [In the sight of the unwise they seemed to die: and their departure is taken for misery] (Wis 3:2).

14.7.2.en: But he whose root waxes old in the earth and whose stock dies in the ground, buds through the scent of water, and that through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, after the pattern of his conduct, and he causes the plant of virtue to grow in the hearts of the elect. For water sometimes signifies the watering of the Holy Spirit, as it is written: "If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink," [whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst] (see Jn 7:37; 4:14).

14.7.3.en: There followed: [and bring forth boughs like a new plant]. It puts forth leaves on the root of the cut tree, for the righteous man dies in the body, and by the example of his sufferings raises the hearts of many, and by his upright faith shows the greenness of truth. Therefore it was well said: [like a new plant]. All that the righteous man does here is a second planting, for it is clear that the first planting does not lie in the practice of goodness but in the foreknowledge of the Creator. While all that the elect do, as if seen for the first time, is settled within them, and afterward is carried out outwardly. It was well said: and bring forth boughs like a new (first) plant, meaning that the greenness appears in the practical carrying out of what was already in the foreknowledge of the Creator.

14.8.0.en: Yet through the scent of water it will bud, and bring forth boughs like a plant [9].

14.8.1.en: If the waters give life to the root of the dead tree, so that it sprouts again and the tree's life returns, then the Holy Spirit gives the believer new life in the waters of baptism. He offers it resurrection, the resurrection of the soul from its death, so that the body also may enjoy the resurrection on the day of the Lord, and the soul may share with the body in eternal life.

14.8.2.en: In the waters of baptism the Holy Spirit brings us into burial with Christ and into resurrection with Him also, so that we come out of baptism members of the body of Christ who rose from the dead, who does not grow old or ancient but grows continually without ceasing, enjoying new life. In this our union with the Lord Christ is realized, so that we enjoy sonship to God, becoming through the only-begotten Son sons with Him by adoption, that is, not by nature, but through free grace. This is what the Apostle meant by his words: "Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us, by the washing of regeneration, and renewing of the Holy Ghost" (Titus 3:5), "Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, which according to his abundant mercy hath begotten us again unto a lively hope by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, to an inheritance incorruptible, and undefiled, and that fadeth not away, reserved in heaven for you" (1 Pet 1:3-4). This is what the Lord Christ Himself meant in His conversation with Nicodemus: "Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born of water and of the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God" (Jn 3:5). And Nicodemus, the teacher of Israel, could not understand, because he had not yet perceived that this Jesus who was speaking to him joins those who believe in Him to Himself in baptism by the Holy Spirit, so as to give them His risen life as the gift of the new spiritual birth.

14.8.3.en: * Was it possible for the rod of the godly Moses to be turned into a serpent, and impossible for the bodies of the godly to live and rise again? And was this done contrary to nature? And will they not return again according to nature?!

14.8.4.en: Likewise the rod of Aaron, though it was cut off, blossomed without scenting water (Job 14:9). Although it was under a roof, it blossomed with flowers as though it were in the fields. Although it was placed in dry places, in one night it bore flowers and the fruit of a plant watered for many years. Did Aaron's rod rise from the dead, and Aaron himself will not rise?!

14.8.5.en: Does God work miracles in wood to secure the priesthood for him, and will He not condescend to raise Aaron himself?

14.8.6.en: St. Cyril of Jerusalem * "Yet through the scent of water it will bud, and bring forth boughs" [9], that is, by the washing of the second birth (Titus 3:5), at the time of the resurrection of the dead. For we have hope of the resurrection, thanks to the grace of baptism. By this we receive a harvest like a new plant, since we are planted in the new Adam (1 Cor 15:45) and are no longer bound to the old Adam. But if old age comes upon us through sloth, if death clings to us through sin, then let us have the scent of water, through weeping like David and Peter and others (2 Sam 12:21; Mt 26:75). For some rightly call the scent of baptism the tears of repentance.

14.8.7.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * When the undivided and unutterable Trinity saw from eternity the fall of human nature, and at the same time brought water into being out of nothing, it prepared for man the healing that was to be accomplished in the waters. This is the reason why, when the Holy Spirit was borne upon the waters, He appeared as sanctifying them... and bound them to the process of begetting (birth). In this it is fitting for us to join the truth together, for it is important to know that at the moment when Jesus was baptized the Holy Spirit came down upon the waves of the Jordan and rested upon them.

14.8.8.en: St. Didymus the Blind * Behold those who are born of God. Here the material womb is the waters of baptism!

14.8.9.en: * We have two births: one earthly, and the other heavenly. The first is from the flesh, and the second from the Spirit.

14.8.10.en: The first proceeds from a perishable principle, and the second from an eternal principle.

14.8.11.en: The first is from a man and a woman, and the second from God and the Church.

14.8.12.en: The first makes us children of the flesh, and the second children of the Spirit.

14.8.13.en: The first makes us children of death, and the second children of the resurrection.

14.8.14.en: The first makes us children of this age, and the second children of God.

14.8.15.en: The first makes us children of the curse and of wrath, and the second children of blessing and love.

14.8.16.en: The first binds us with the chains of original sin, and the second looses us from the bonds of every sin.

14.8.17.en: St. Augustine But man dieth, and wasteth away.

14.9.0.en: Yea, man giveth up the ghost, and where is he! [10]

14.9.1.en: When man dies the body wastes away and perishes, becoming like dust, and the spirit departs and no longer returns to the body in this world.

14.9.2.en: Although some of Job's words in the book seem to be those of one who does not believe in the resurrection, here he calls death a sleep and the resurrection an awakening from lying down, which confirms his living faith in the resurrection from the dead.

14.9.3.en: * [When man dies and is stripped and perishes, I ask: where is he?] [10] There is no man without sin except the One who came into the world without sin. And while we are all bound by iniquity, we die by losing righteousness.

14.9.4.en: The garment of innocence was given to us formerly in Paradise, and we were stripped of it and became naked. This nakedness of the prodigal son the Father granted to be covered, for He said at his return: [Bring forth quickly the first robe] (see Lk 15:22).

14.9.5.en: For the first robe is the garment of innocence, which man rightly received at his creation, but when he was deceived by the serpent he lost it.

14.9.6.en: Again it is said of this nakedness: [Blessed is he that watcheth, and keepeth his garments, lest he walk naked] (Rev 16:15). For we keep our garments when we keep the commandments of innocence in our hearts, so that if we have been stripped and appear naked before the Judge because of iniquity, by repentance we are covered and the innocence we lost returns to us.

14.9.7.en: It was well said: "I ask where is he?" for the sinner does not stand there where he was created, while here, where he fell, he is prevented from standing long. By his own will he lost his homeland, and against his will he is drawn out of his exile, in which he rejoices. Then where is this one in whom there is no love of God, where is the truth of his being?
